sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Each example contains the correction, not just the answer.

items.prompt: A data set is: 17, 25, 16, 22, with a mean of 20. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of this data set?

steps: Find each value's distance from the mean: |17-20| = 3, |25-20| = 5, |16-20| = 4, |22-20| = 2.
Divide by the number of values: 14 ÷ 4 = 3 1/2.

items.prompt: Two data sets have means of 30 and 42. Their mean absolute deviation (MAD) is 4. Express the difference between the means as a multiple of the MAD.

steps: Find the difference between the means: 42 − 30 = 12.
The means differ by 3 times the MAD.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Before solving, say which error the problem is testing for.

items.prompt: Sample A: 17, 21, 22, 28. Sample B: 39, 40, 31, 30. Based on the means, which sample tends to have greater values?
choices: Sample A, with a mean of 22 compared to 35.
Both samples have the same mean.
Sample B, with a mean of 35 compared to 22.
Sample B, with a mean of 22 compared to 35.

items.prompt: Sample A: 18, 17, 19, 17, 19. Sample B: 16, 10, 28, 11, 13. Based on the range of each sample, which sample is more consistent (less variable)?
choices: Sample B, with a range of 18 compared to 2.
Both samples have the same range.
Sample A, with a range of 18 compared to 2.
Sample A, with a range of 2 compared to 18.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know about all 241 students at Lincoln Middle School. She randomly selects 37 of them to survey. What is the population in this situation?
choices: The researcher's own estimate
Only the first 37 students at Lincoln Middle School on a list
The 37 randomly selected students at Lincoln Middle School
All 241 students at Lincoln Middle School

items.prompt: A student picks a random starting point, then surveys every 10th person from the full numbered list of visitors to a science museum, for a total of 48. Is this sampling method likely to produce a representative sample?
choices: No, likely not representative, because the population is too large.
Yes, likely representative, because the sample size is large enough.
Yes, likely representative — every member had a fair, known chance of being chosen.
No, likely not representative — the method favors certain members over others.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: In a random sample of 13 visitors to a science museum, 6 preferred a new park design. Based on this sample, about how many of the 52 visitors to a science museum would you expect to prefer a new park design?
Five random samples of the same population produced these mean scores: 16, 18, 6, 5, 13. What is the range of these sample estimates?

A population has 2934 shoppers at a grocery store. Student A takes a random sample of 53. Student B takes a random sample of 12. Both use proper random selection. Whose sample is more likely to give an estimate closer to the true population value?
choices: Student A's sample of 53, because larger random samples tend to produce more consistent, accurate estimates.
Both are equally likely to be accurate, because both are random.
Student B's sample of 12, because smaller samples are easier to analyze.
Neither sample is reliable unless it includes the entire population.

items.prompt: A student surveys 54 commuters on a train line using a convenience sample of her classmates only and records the results. Is it valid to generalize this result to all 2322 commuters on a train line?
choices: Yes, because the sample was selected randomly, so it is likely representative of the population.
No, because samples can never be generalized to a population.
No, because the sample was not randomly selected, so it may not represent the population.
Yes, because the sample size is large enough regardless of how it was chosen.
